value.description: Machine-readable knowledge graph of Git's history, architecture, object model, refs, commands, merge algorithms, transports, server/hosting ecosystem, extensions, workflows, implementations and security lessons.

value.name: Local edit-to-commit lifecycle
value.description: Stages a selected working-tree state and records it as a new snapshot in local history.

steps.action: Edit files in the working tree
effects: working_tree changes
index updated
new commit and tree objects
current branch ref advances
review local history and remaining changes

value.name: Distributed collaboration lifecycle
value.description: Copies repository history locally, develops a branch, and publishes it to a remote repository.

effects: local repository and working tree created
branch ref points to current commit
local commits extend branch history
remote-tracking refs and objects updated
remote receives commits/ref if policy permits

steps.action: Request review through hosting service if used
effects: pull/merge request opened outside core Git

value.name: Merge and conflict-resolution workflow
value.description: Integrates divergent branch histories using a merge strategy and asks for manual resolution when necessary.

effects: remote state becomes available locally
Git calculates merge result from history/common ancestor
manual edits reconcile competing changes
index records resolutions
merge commit records multiple parents where applicable

value.name: Object storage and packing lifecycle
value.description: Represents files and snapshots as immutable content-addressed objects, then compacts objects into packfiles.

effects: blob IDs derive from content hashes
tree entries link names/modes to blobs and subtrees
commit references root tree and parent commits
fast object creation, more filesystem entries
packfiles and indexes improve storage/transfer efficiency
integrity/connectivity checks run

value.name: Release authentication pattern
value.description: Use an annotated signed tag to identify and authenticate a release point.

effects: release state exists in history
tag object contains metadata and signature
remote receives tag subject to policy

steps.action: Verify signer and tag before consuming release
effects: signature verification supports publisher authentication

value.name: Prevent and remediate secret exposure
value.description: Reduce the chance that credentials are committed and define remediation if a secret enters history.

steps.action: Ignore local secret/config files where appropriate
effects: untracked matching files are excluded

steps.action: Use secret scanning and pre-commit checks
effects: credentials can be detected before publication

steps.action: If a secret was committed, revoke or rotate it immediately
effects: exposed credential is no longer trusted

steps.action: Coordinate history cleanup and remote cleanup
effects: sensitive content may be removed by history rewrite, but clones/caches may retain copies

steps.action: Use revert rather than rewriting ordinary shared history
effects: published shared history remains stable for routine changes

value.name: Secure repository transport and authorization
value.description: Separate transport security from repository authorization and signed-history verification.

effects: protects transport and/or authenticates remote depending on configuration

steps.action: Enforce repository permissions at server/hosting layer
effects: read/write access constrained by policy

steps.action: Review untrusted clone URLs, submodule URLs and hooks
effects: reduces malicious repository/config execution risk

steps.action: Verify signed release tags or commits when provided
effects: authenticates signer for signed content; hashes alone do not prove identity
receives security fixes for known vulnerabilities

value.name: Fork-and-review workflow
value.description: Uses an independent repository and hosting-service pull request for collaboration.

steps.action: Fork or clone the upstream repository
effects: independent development copy created

steps.action: Develop commits on a topic branch
effects: change history isolated from upstream default branch

steps.action: Push branch to a writable remote
effects: branch becomes available for review

steps.action: Open pull/merge request on hosting service
effects: review metadata and discussion tracked by forge

steps.action: Review, test and merge through configured process
effects: approved commits integrated into target branch

value.name: Large repository optimization
value.description: Use packing, selective transfer and virtualization/extensions when repository size becomes expensive.

effects: reduced loose-object overhead and delta-compressed storage
fetch can request only relevant refs

steps.action: Use Git LFS for appropriate large binary assets
effects: large payloads handled through LFS workflows

steps.action: Consider VFS for Git for huge working trees
effects: placeholder files downloaded when accessed

steps.action: Measure repository history and clone costs
effects: choose optimization based on workload

value.title: Local commits are repository-local until published
value.statement: A successful local commit does not automatically update a remote repository; use push or an explicit hosting workflow to publish changes.

value.title: Review the index before committing
value.statement: git commit records staged content, so inspect staged diffs and status to avoid committing unintended changes.

value.title: A content hash is not publisher authentication
value.statement: Object hashes support content identity and integrity checks, but signed tags/commits or a trusted release process are needed to authenticate who published content.

value.title: Do not assume SHA-1 collision resistance
value.statement: The source documents the SHAttered demonstration and Git's hash-transition work; deployments should follow current Git guidance on hash compatibility and security.

value.title: Do not treat .gitignore as secret removal
value.statement: Ignoring a file prevents matching untracked files from being added by ordinary workflows; it does not erase already committed secrets from history or other clones.

value.title: Rotate exposed credentials before history cleanup
value.statement: If a credential was committed, revoke/rotate it first; history rewriting alone cannot ensure every clone or cache has discarded the value.

value.title: Prefer revert for changes already shared
value.statement: A new revert commit is generally safer for shared published history than rewriting commits on which others may depend.

value.title: Enforce permissions outside core Git
value.statement: Git's core does not provide access control; enforce read/write authorization at the server, SSH, hosting or authorization-tool layer.

value.title: Treat untrusted repositories as executable-risk inputs
value.statement: Inspect repository configuration, hooks, submodule URLs and scripts before running commands or tools from untrusted repositories.

value.title: Use authenticated protected transports for remotes
value.statement: Prefer appropriately configured SSH or HTTPS and verify host identity; an unencrypted or untrusted transport can expose users to redirection or interception.

value.title: Keep Git clients and servers patched
value.statement: Historical vulnerabilities were fixed in later releases; update supported clients, servers and hosting services to receive security fixes.

value.title: Do not rely on unreachable objects as durable backups
value.statement: Unreachable objects may be removed by automatic or explicit garbage collection; preserve important commits with refs or backups.

value.title: Rename history is inferred, not stored as permanent file identity
value.statement: Git detects renames heuristically while viewing history; a rename with substantial simultaneous edits may appear as deletion plus addition.

value.title: Pull requests belong to hosting/workflow layers
value.statement: A pull request is not a native Git object or command; Git transports commits and refs while hosting services manage review records and merge UI.

value.title: Validate merges that require manual conflict resolution
value.statement: A successful merge operation can still require human judgment; test the integrated result and review staged resolutions before finalizing.

value.title: Limit unnecessary ref advertisement in large repositories
value.statement: Where supported, protocol v2 allows clients to request relevant refs, reducing overhead for fetches that need only a subset of repository state.

value.title: Verify signatures for security-sensitive releases
value.statement: When a release uses signed tags, verify the signature and trust in the signing key before relying on the tag as publisher-authenticated.

value.title: Distinguish working tree, index and object database
value.statement: Working-tree edits are not staged; staged content is not committed; committed objects are local history until pushed.

value.title: Do not assume every repository uses the same default branch name
value.statement: Repositories may use main, master or a configured alternative; inspect local and remote refs rather than hard-coding a branch name.

value.title: Create and commit a local change
value.scenario: A developer changes a file and wants a recorded snapshot.
value.outcome: The index contents become a new commit in local history; nothing is published remotely unless pushed.

value.title: Collaborate on a feature branch
value.scenario: A developer contributes a feature to a shared repository.
steps: open a pull/merge request on the hosting service
value.outcome: Commits remain locally available offline, then are published to a remote branch and optionally reviewed using a hosting-layer pull request.

value.title: Resolve conflicting edits
value.scenario: Two branches modify overlapping lines and Git cannot automatically choose a result.
steps: edit files to desired combined result
value.outcome: The resulting history records the integrated state; tests and review are needed to validate semantic correctness.

value.title: Authenticate a release tag
value.scenario: A maintainer wants consumers to verify that a release tag was signed by an expected key.
value.outcome: Signature verification checks the tag signature; consumers must also trust the signer/key and verify release provenance.

value.title: Respond to a committed credential
value.scenario: A password or API token accidentally enters a commit and may have been pushed.
steps: Revoke or rotate the credential immediately
Check access logs and downstream use
Coordinate removal/rewriting of affected history if required
Notify collaborators and clean relevant clones/caches where feasible
Add preventive scanning and appropriate ignore rules
value.outcome: The credential is invalidated first; history cleanup reduces future exposure but cannot guarantee every copy is erased.

value.title: Inspect repository integrity and storage
value.scenario: A maintainer wants to check object connectivity and reduce loose-object overhead.
value.outcome: Integrity checks and object packing can reveal repository issues and improve storage efficiency; garbage collection can prune unreachable objects.

fields.label: Notes
value: Git is distributed even when a team chooses a central integration server.
Git's content-addressed object store, commit-parent links and tree structure form the basis of its history and integrity model.
Hashes do not by themselves establish the identity or trustworthiness of a publisher; signatures and trusted key distribution address that separate problem.
Hosting features such as pull requests and fine-grained authorization are distinct from core Git objects and commands.

Some source details are explicitly historical (e.g., recursive merge strategy, SHA-1 internals, old vulnerabilities, and planned Git 3.0 default branch change); verify current official documentation before relying on them operationally.

value.name: Compilation pipeline
value.formula: Go source → compiler → linker → native binary → CPU/OS
value.mechanism: Compiler and linker produce statically linked native artifacts containing the Go runtime.

value.name: Package/dependency model
value.formula: module → package path → import → exported API → dependency graph
value.mechanism: Packages are identified by paths; modules and go mod manage dependencies.

value.name: Interface satisfaction
value.formula: T + required methods(I) → T satisfies I
value.mechanism: No implements declaration is needed; method sets determine satisfaction.

value.name: Generic instantiation
value.formula: generic definition + type arguments/inference → instantiated code
value.mechanism: Type parameters, constraints and compiler instantiation provide generic code.

value.name: Goroutine scheduling
value.formula: goroutines → runtime scheduler → OS threads → CPUs
value.mechanism: Runtime multiplexes lightweight goroutines over fewer OS threads.

value.name: Channel communication
value.formula: goroutine A → typed channel → goroutine B
value.mechanism: Typed send/receive and select coordinate concurrent execution.

value.name: Concurrency memory model
value.mechanism: Unsynchronized sharing may race; synchronization is required for safe concurrent access.

value.name: Error-value model
value.mechanism: Multiple returns make explicit error handling the normal package-boundary mechanism.

value.name: HTTP application model
value.mechanism: Standard library provides handlers and server startup.

value.name: Integrated development workflow
value.formula: source → gofmt → build → test → vet → doc/generate → deploy
value.mechanism: Go distribution integrates common software-engineering tasks.

value.name: Go infrastructure ecosystem
value.mechanism: Named major applications demonstrate Go infrastructure reach.

value.name: Tony Hoare
value.role: CSP model referenced as concurrency influence

value.distinction: Concurrency can exploit parallel CPUs but is not identical to parallel processing.
Go interface conformance is statically checked, so structural typing is more precise.
Interfaces provide polymorphism without a class hierarchy.
Array length is part of its type; slices provide dynamic length/capacity.
Ordinary pointers lack arithmetic; unsafe.Pointer is the special escape hatch.
Errors are normal; panic/recover is exceptional.
Goroutines are multiplexed onto OS threads.
Modules organize dependencies; packages organize importable code.
Slices are sequences; maps are key/value mappings.
Go keeps C-like foundations while simplifying and changing safety/type/concurrency mechanisms.
Go source is compiled and linked into native artifacts.
Go normally manages memory with GC.

value.misconception: Go concurrency prevents data races.
value.correction: Goroutines share an address space and unsynchronized access can race.

value.misconception: Interfaces require implements declarations.
value.correction: Interfaces are satisfied implicitly by matching methods.

value.misconception: Go interfaces are dynamic duck typing.
value.correction: Interface satisfaction is statically checked structural typing.

value.misconception: Slice is just a dynamic array.
value.correction: Slice is a distinct type with length/capacity over underlying storage.

value.misconception: Go has C-style pointer arithmetic.
value.correction: Ordinary pointer arithmetic is absent; unsafe.Pointer is special.

value.misconception: Go normally uses exceptions.
value.correction: Error values and multiple returns are conventional.

value.misconception: Go is only for web services.
value.correction: Source names containers, orchestration, databases and static-site generation too.

value.misconception: Go is interpreted.
value.correction: Go is compiled into native binaries.

value.misconception: Go always had generics.
value.correction: Generics arrived in Go 1.18.

value.misconception: Go is just C with GC.
value.correction: Go changes types, concurrency, packages and language features substantially.

formal_models.name: Goroutine scheduling
formal_models.formula: goroutines → runtime scheduler → OS threads → CPUs
formal_models.mechanism: Runtime multiplexes lightweight goroutines over fewer OS threads.

formal_models.name: Channel communication
formal_models.formula: goroutine A → typed channel → goroutine B
formal_models.mechanism: Typed send/receive and select coordinate concurrent execution.

formal_models.name: Concurrency memory model
formal_models.mechanism: Unsynchronized sharing may race; synchronization is required for safe concurrent access.

formal_models.name: Error-value model
formal_models.mechanism: Multiple returns make explicit error handling the normal package-boundary mechanism.

formal_models.name: HTTP application model
formal_models.mechanism: Standard library provides handlers and server startup.

source_claims.claim: Go is a high-level general-purpose statically typed compiled language with GC and concurrency.
Go was designed at Google for productivity on multicore/networked machines and large codebases.
Go has a self-hosting toolchain and a C++ frontend supporting GCC/LLVM.
Go simplifies C-style syntax with short declarations, multiple returns and range iteration.
Go provides arrays, slices, pointers, maps, channels, structs, methods and interfaces.
Interfaces use structural satisfaction without implements declarations.
Generics with type parameters and constraints arrived in Go 1.18.
Packages use paths/visibility and modules manage dependencies.
Goroutines, channels and select provide built-in concurrency.
Shared memory can race; race detection is available.
Go is used for Caddy, Docker, Kubernetes, CockroachDB, Hugo and TypeScript 7.
Go deliberately omits inheritance, assertions, pointer arithmetic and implicit conversions.
Go 1 prioritizes backward compatibility and does not plan Go 2.0.

named_people.name: Tony Hoare
named_people.role: CSP model referenced as concurrency influence

semantic_distinctions.distinction: Concurrency can exploit parallel CPUs but is not identical to parallel processing.
Go interface conformance is statically checked, so structural typing is more precise.
Interfaces provide polymorphism without a class hierarchy.
Array length is part of its type; slices provide dynamic length/capacity.
Ordinary pointers lack arithmetic; unsafe.Pointer is the special escape hatch.
Errors are normal; panic/recover is exceptional.
Goroutines are multiplexed onto OS threads.
Modules organize dependencies; packages organize importable code.
Slices are sequences; maps are key/value mappings.
Go keeps C-like foundations while simplifying and changing safety/type/concurrency mechanisms.
Go source is compiled and linked into native artifacts.
Go normally manages memory with GC.

misconceptions.misconception: Go concurrency prevents data races.
misconceptions.correction: Goroutines share an address space and unsynchronized access can race.

misconceptions.misconception: Interfaces require implements declarations.
misconceptions.correction: Interfaces are satisfied implicitly by matching methods.

misconceptions.misconception: Go interfaces are dynamic duck typing.
misconceptions.correction: Interface satisfaction is statically checked structural typing.

misconceptions.misconception: Slice is just a dynamic array.
misconceptions.correction: Slice is a distinct type with length/capacity over underlying storage.

misconceptions.misconception: Go has C-style pointer arithmetic.
misconceptions.correction: Ordinary pointer arithmetic is absent; unsafe.Pointer is special.

misconceptions.misconception: Go normally uses exceptions.
misconceptions.correction: Error values and multiple returns are conventional.

misconceptions.misconception: Go is only for web services.
misconceptions.correction: Source names containers, orchestration, databases and static-site generation too.

misconceptions.misconception: Go is interpreted.
misconceptions.correction: Go is compiled into native binaries.

misconceptions.misconception: Go always had generics.
misconceptions.correction: Generics arrived in Go 1.18.

misconceptions.misconception: Go is just C with GC.
misconceptions.correction: Go changes types, concurrency, packages and language features substantially.

value.name: Resource addressing model
value.meaning: Resources are identified through URI/URL and represented in messages.

value.name: HTTP/1.1 message model
value.expression: start-line + header-fields + CRLF delimiter + optional body
value.meaning: HTTP/1.1 message structure described in the source.

value.name: HTTP/2 multiplexing model
value.expression: one TCP/IP connection -> multiple bidirectional streams -> concurrent requests/responses
value.meaning: HTTP/2 shares a connection across streams.

value.name: HTTP/3 transport model
value.meaning: HTTP/3 replaces TCP transport with QUIC over UDP.

value.name: Caching model
value.expression: request -> cache lookup -> reuse or conditional retrieval -> response
value.meaning: Caches and conditional requests reduce repeated network transfer.

value.name: HTTP authentication model
value.expression: server challenge -> client credentials -> access decision

value.name: Status classification model
value.meaning: Response disposition is classified by status-code class.

value.name: Method semantics model
value.expression: method -> intended action + safety + idempotence + cacheability
value.meaning: HTTP methods have defined semantic properties.

value.name: Persistent connection model
value.expression: one TCP connection -> multiple HTTP requests/responses
value.meaning: HTTP/1.1 keep-alive reduces repeated TCP setup.

value.name: Range retrieval model
value.meaning: Byte serving retrieves selected portions and can resume interrupted downloads.

value.name: Application session model
value.expression: stateless HTTP + cookie/hidden variable/etc. -> application session
value.meaning: Sessions are implemented above HTTP's stateless protocol semantics.

value.difference: HTTPS is the secure variant of HTTP.
HTTP/1.1 supports reusable persistent connections; HTTP/1.0 normally closed after response.
HTTP/2 uses binary framing and multiplexed streams rather than HTTP/1.1's textual message exchange.
HTTP/2 uses TCP; HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP.
Hop-by-hop headers can be managed by intermediaries; end-to-end headers are managed only by endpoints.
Safe means no intended server-state effect; idempotent means repeated identical requests have the same intended effect.
Cacheability is whether responses may be stored; it is distinct from safety.
GET retrieves a representation and is safe/cacheable; POST processes a resource and is not safe/idempotent by definition.
PUT supplies state for create/update at client-specified target; PATCH applies partial state.
HTTP authentication belongs to protocol access control; application login/session is application-level.
A resource is the target concept; a representation is the data form returned for it.
Header names are case-insensitive; method names are case-sensitive.
Status codes are machine-readable; reason phrases are human-readable recommendations.
Persistent reuse keeps a connection open; pipelining sends multiple requests before responses and had interoperability problems.
Chunked transfer supports unknown-length streaming; Content-Length explicitly states known length.
Byte ranges retrieve only selected portions.
TCP is the traditional reliable transport; QUIC provides reliability over UDP for HTTP/3.
HTTP/0.9 was extremely minimal, with only GET and HTML responses.
SPDY was an alternative Google protocol whose ideas influenced HTTP/2.
The source describes HTTP as displacing Gopher for content delivery in the early 1990s.

value.misconception: HTTP itself is TCP.
value.correction: HTTP is an application protocol; TCP is a traditional underlying transport, while HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP.

value.misconception: HTTP/3 is just HTTP/2 with a different version number.
value.correction: HTTP/3 changes the transport model to QUIC over UDP.

value.misconception: HTTP is stateful because websites have logins.
value.correction: HTTP itself is stateless; application sessions add state above HTTP.

value.misconception: Safe means idempotent and idempotent means safe.
value.correction: They overlap for several methods but describe different semantic properties.

value.misconception: GET can never cause side effects.
value.correction: The source says implementations can misuse GET; safe describes intended semantics, not technical enforcement.

value.misconception: POST is idempotent.
value.correction: The source explicitly says POST is not necessarily idempotent.

value.misconception: All HTTP methods are cacheable.
value.correction: The source defines only GET, HEAD and POST as cacheable.

value.misconception: HTTP/1.1 always opens a new TCP connection for every resource.
value.correction: HTTP/1.1 can reuse persistent connections.

value.misconception: HTTP/2 sends multiple independent TCP connections for every request.
value.correction: The source describes multiplexed streams over a shared TCP/IP connection.

value.misconception: HTTP/3 uses TCP underneath QUIC.
value.correction: QUIC runs over UDP.

value.misconception: Header field names and method names use the same case rules.
value.correction: Methods are case-sensitive; header field names are case-insensitive.

value.misconception: A response body is always present.
value.correction: The body is optional.

value.misconception: A resource is always a static file.
value.correction: The source says resources may be files or dynamically generated/executable output.

value.misconception: Authentication and application login are the same HTTP mechanism.
value.correction: The source distinguishes HTTP authentication from application-session login.

value.misconception: HTTP/0.9 supported POST and arbitrary content formats.
value.correction: The source says HTTP/0.9 supported only GET and returned HTML pages.

value.misconception: HTTP/2 made HTTP/1.1 obsolete.
value.correction: The source describes HTTP/2 as an evolution while HTTP/1.1 remains a standard version.

value.misconception: HTTPS is a different application protocol unrelated to HTTP.
value.correction: HTTPS is described as the secure variant of HTTP.

value.misconception: Byte-range serving always downloads the whole resource.
value.correction: It retrieves selected portions and can resume interrupted downloads.

value.misconception: Chunked transfer requires Content-Length.
value.correction: Chunked transfer is specifically useful when length is not known in advance.

value.misconception: Status reason phrases are the machine-readable part of responses.
value.correction: Status codes are machine-readable; reason phrases are human-readable.

source_claims.statement: HTTP is an application-layer protocol in the Internet protocol suite for distributed, collaborative hypermedia information systems.
HTTP is foundational to World Wide Web data communication.
HTTP uses request-response in the client-server model.
Browsers, crawlers, voice browsers, mobile apps and other software can act as user agents.
HTTP supports intermediate caches and proxies; some headers are hop-by-hop and others end-to-end.
Web resources are located through URL/URI schemes http and https.
HTTP/0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 2 and 3 are the versions listed with their introduction years/statuses.
HTTP/1.0 used a separate TCP connection per resource; HTTP/1.1 introduced reusable persistent connections.
HTTP/2 adds binary header representation, multiplexed streams, and server push.
HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP rather than TCP.
HTTP data exchange uses reliable transport; TCP is the pre-HTTP/3 standard choice.
HTTP/1.1 messages have start line, header fields, blank line, and optional body.
HTTP methods classify requested actions and have safety, idempotence, and cacheability properties.
GET is intended to retrieve without modifying server state, while other methods can modify state.
Safe methods are GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE and QUERY in the supplied source.
Idempotent methods include PUT, DELETE and safe methods; POST, CONNECT and PATCH are not necessarily idempotent.
GET, HEAD and POST are defined as cacheable in the source table.
HTTP response status codes are three-digit classes 1xx through 5xx.
HTTP is stateless; application sessions can be implemented with cookies, hidden variables or other mechanisms.
HTTP provides Basic and Digest authentication through challenge-response.
HTTPS is the popular encrypted form of HTTP.
HTTP/1.1 message headers use ASCII lines terminated by CRLF.
HTTP/1.1 supports conditional retrieval, chunked transfer and byte-range serving.
Tim Berners-Lee and CERN are credited with HTTP's invention/development.
HTTP/0.9 supported only GET and returned HTML pages.
SPDY influenced HTTP/2 and was developed by Google.
HTTP/2 was published in 2015 and HTTP/3 was standardized in 2022.
RFC 9110/9111/9112/9113/9114 are the current semantic/caching/version documents listed by the source.

metadata.title: Imperative Programming Paradigm — Comprehensive Knowledge Graph
metadata.subject: Imperative programming, its core concepts, history, languages, implementations, tools, and application domains
source_basis: Established general knowledge used to expand the language inventory and connect concepts beyond the excerpt

source_handling.uploaded_source: The uploaded article is treated as the source for its described paradigm, procedural programming, state and control-flow concepts, and named historical examples.
source_handling.expanded_knowledge: The language inventory and many implementation/runtime connections are expanded using general model knowledge; individual release milestones and lineage links may require source-specific verification.
source_handling.scope_note: Imperative is a broad paradigm. Languages listed may be multi-paradigm and are included because they support substantial imperative programming, not because they are exclusively imperative.

metadata.relationship_direction: Every relationship is directed from source to target; reciprocal meaning is represented by a separate relationship when appropriate.
metadata.identifier_conventions: Entity IDs use descriptive snake_case; relationship IDs are sequential rel_00001-style identifiers.
coverage_notes: Paradigm definition and contrast with declarative programming
Procedural, structured, object-oriented, event-driven, reactive, concurrent, and functional connections
State, mutation, side effects, assignments, expressions, procedures, functions, scope, control flow, loops, branches, exceptions, I/O
Memory regions, allocation, garbage collection, ownership, RAII, and resource lifetimes
Compilers, interpreters, virtual machines, bytecode, JIT/AOT, linking, build systems, testing, and debugging
Broad inventory of imperative and multi-paradigm languages, including historical, mainstream, scripting, systems, and domain-oriented examples
Designers, institutions, standards, operating systems, processor architectures, runtimes, and application domains
Relations are explanatory knowledge-graph edges, not a claim that every language implements every feature identically
